$comment: The in-repo record of which CI checks can stop a merge to `main`, and why
the rest cannot (#542). Ruleset 16189198 carried no `required_status_checks`
rule at all, so every check was advisory: PR #540 merged while markdownlint
was reporting FAILURE and `main` went red until #541.
Direction of authority differs by section, so read that first. For the
REQUIRED SET this file is PRIMARY (ADR 0011): it is declared here and
applied to the ruleset, and the GitHub ruleset is the copy that enforces
it. For everything under `rulesetRules` — and for `strict` in
`mergePolicy` — this file is OBSERVATIONAL: those are not applied from
here, so on a disagreement the RULESET WINS and this file is the wrong
one. `ts/test/workflow-false-green.test.ts` keeps the two
honest against the workflows: every `required` check must be produced by a
workflow that runs unconditionally on `pull_request` (a required check behind
a `paths:` filter never reports, and the PR can never merge), and every
check-producing job must appear here as either required or advisory with a
stated reason. A new job that is neither fails the suite rather than joining
the advisory pile by default.
ADR 0010: a check is promoted once its precision is known. That is a real
reason to wait. `nobody configured it` is not, and is what #542 was filed
about.
To apply this file to the ruleset:
gh api -X PUT repos/bop-clocktower/canary/rulesets/16189198 --input <payload>
See docs/knowledge/decisions/0011-required-status-checks.md for the procedure.
#678 — the confirmed reason a PR-time check can pass while the identical
commit fails post-merge. Read against the live ruleset with:
gh api repos/bop-clocktower/canary/rulesets/16189198
`strict` is GitHub's `strict_required_status_checks_policy`. With it
FALSE a PR merges without being up to date with `main`. Combined with the
default `actions/checkout` behaviour on `pull_request` — which checks out
the merge commit GitHub computed for that event, i.e. head merged into
`main` as of the last push to the PR BRANCH — a green check is a verdict
about `merge(head, main@t0)`. Nothing re-runs when the base moves to t1,
because base movement fires no check run on the PR. So the PR-time green
and the post-merge red were answers to two different questions, and the
gate was reporting after the fact rather than gating. #660 is the worked
example: its own `harness` check passed, the same commit failed
`check-arch` on `main`, and #663 inherited the failure and read as its
cause.
RESOLVED: `strict` is TRUE on the ruleset, so the case above is closed
— a PR cannot merge until its branch is up to date, and the green it
merges on is a verdict about the tree that actually lands.
Since when: the ruleset has not been edited since 2026-08-12T23:21-05:00
(`updated_at`), so `strict` has been true since at least then. This file
recorded `false` in 6fe3b60 at 23:15 the same evening — six minutes
earlier — and stayed wrong until 2026-09-03. Three weeks, noticed only
because a merge was refused for a reason this file said could not happen.
Note the direction of authority, which differs per field and is the
reason this drifted. ADR 0011 makes the manifest primary for the
REQUIRED SET: that is declared here and applied to the ruleset, and the
test suite checks it against the workflows. `strict` is not applied from
this file — it is set on the ruleset — so for this one field the manifest
is an OBSERVATION, and observations go stale silently. On a disagreement
about `strict`, the ruleset wins and this line is the wrong one.
The cost the earlier note predicted is real and is now the operating
condition: every open PR goes stale whenever `main` moves, so a queue of
concurrent PRs has to be updated and re-run one at a time. Repo-level
auto-merge is enabled to absorb that, but it does NOT update a branch
for you — it waits, so a stale PR sits until something calls
`gh pr update-branch`. A merge queue is the feature that removes the
manual step; this ruleset carries no `merge_queue` rule, so that is an
option not taken rather than one not considered.
Defence in depth, and still wanted now that `strict` is true: every
workflow producing a required check also runs on `push: main`, so a
stale green — from `strict` regressing, an actor being added to a
currently empty `bypass_actors`, or the required-checks rule being
edited — is caught on `main` within one run rather than surfacing as
the NEXT PR's failure. (No bypass exists today: `bypass_actors` is
empty and `enforcement` is active, so even a direct push from
`github-actions[bot]` is rejected.)
`guardian.yml` is the sole exemption — it reviews a pull-request diff
and has nothing to say about a push.

required.check: Code fences open and close correctly

$comment: RENAMED from `enforce` by #698; the workflow's display name changed
from `Architecture Enforcer` to `Dependency & project validation` in
the same commit. The old name asserted a job that does NOT exist: the
steps are `harness check-deps` and `harness validate`, and neither
reads `.harness/arch/baselines.json`. The architecture ratchet lives in
the `harness` check above, via `harness ci check` plus the `check-arch`
detail report that `scripts/arch-verdict.mjs` classifies. That is why
this job could be green while a local `harness check-arch` exited 1
with 21 threshold violations (#678): different commands, not one gate
disagreeing with itself. The previous entry here annotated the lie
(#697); this one removes it.
The context string is the JOB ID, because the job sets no `name:`. It
is also an entry in ruleset 16189198, which this file does not edit —
the swap was applied by hand with the `gh api -X PUT` line in the
header. A required context that no longer reports blocks every PR
forever, so the workflow, this file, and the ruleset must never be
allowed to disagree about this string.
The more ambitious fix — making the name true by adding `harness
check-arch` here — was considered and rejected in #698: the ratchet
reports 21 pre-existing threshold violations, so requiring it would
block every merge until those are allowanced. That is a separate
decision and must not ride along with a rename.

advisory.reason: Advisory by design until the #486 exit criterion is met on measured evidence: 20 consecutive mutant-producing PRs at a false-survivor rate <= 10% with p90 runtime inside the 10-minute budget (spec D5). Today it can only abstain, and does so loudly: @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner 10.0.0 runs zero tests per mutant on vitest 5 (stryker-js#6210), so a run under it would report every covered mutant as survived. Note the job exits 0 on survivors BUT the command itself exits 1, and an abstention exits 3 rather than passing -- what is advisory is the blocking, never the denominator.

Reports only (#836, ADR 0022): it prints the remote branch deletion set and deletes nothing, so there is nothing to block on. It depends on the GitHub API for PR state, and an API flake must not read as a code failure. It still fails loudly when it abstains (exit 3), because that means the checkout had no remote refs to classify.

Precision not yet known (ADR 0010). The dogfood jobs run canary against canary and currently report a 409-finding baseline that #544 has not triaged. Promoting before the triage would block every PR on findings nobody has confirmed are real.

Step 1 of the two-step #843 migration (ADR 0023). pull_request_target runs the base branch's workflow, so this job cannot report on the PR that introduces it; the required context `No removed-symbol or proprietary leaks` stays on docs-lint.yml until step 2 renames this job to it and removes the docs-lint.yml job. Advisory only for that transition window.
Same dogfood baseline as above (#544). Also exercises a packed npm install, which depends on registry availability — a network flake would read as a code failure.
Same dogfood baseline as above (#544). Promote alongside the other dogfood jobs once the baseline is triaged rather than one at a time.

New in this batch and never run against the corpus before, so its precision is unknown (ADR 0010). The first sweep reports 1 finding (canary-shadow documents no runnable command) and 29 of 33 documented examples as unverifiable; promoting before that backlog is triaged would block every PR on findings nobody has confirmed. Note the job DOES fail on a collapsed denominator even while advisory — an abstention is not a finding whose precision is in question, it is the check reporting it measured nothing.
Reports on accumulated run history, so its verdict depends on prior runs rather than on this PR's diff. A required check must be a function of the change under review.
Advisory by design — canary-katana records deleted and skipped tests and alarms only when the deletion removes the last coverage of a high-risk symbol. Same dogfood baseline (#544).

Not a gate. Triggers only on `pull_request: types: [labeled]` — an on-demand action a maintainer invokes to refresh the architecture baseline. It does not report on an ordinary PR, so requiring it would deadlock every PR that is never labeled.

$comment: #769. Commit statuses posted by a GitHub App rather than by a workflow in
`.github/workflows/`. They sit outside the `required`/`advisory` lists
above BY CONSTRUCTION, because those are keyed to a producing workflow —
which is exactly why one of them could be red on every commit for weeks
with nothing in the repo accounting for it.
`ts/test/workflow-false-green.test.ts` enumerates PR checks by parsing
workflow YAML, so an app-produced context is invisible to it. This list
is the denominator that check cannot compute for itself: every entry
states who produces the status, whether it can block a merge, and what is
being done about it. An entry whose `expected` is `none` asserts the app
should stop posting at all — if the status reappears, the suppression
regressed and this file is the record of what was supposed to happen.

reason: canary is a CLI and skills toolkit with no deployable web surface, so
a Vercel project connected to this repo has nothing it can build. The
status reported FAILURE on every PR and on `main` from 3659ea9
onward. It is NOT in ruleset 16189198's required contexts, so it
blocks nothing — and that is the whole problem. A check that is
ALWAYS red is indistinguishable from a check that is red because
something broke, so it trains reviewers to skim past a red X. That is
the signal erosion #542 was filed about, arriving from the opposite
direction: there nothing could stop a merge, here something always
looks like it should.
Repo-side fix: `vercel.json` declares `git.deploymentEnabled: false`,
the documented lever that makes the Git integration skip creating a
deployment for any branch. No deployment means no commit status.
NOT fixed from the repo: the project remains CONNECTED in the Vercel
dashboard, and only a maintainer with dashboard access can disconnect
it. `vercel.json` suppresses the symptom from inside the repo, which
is the durable half — it travels with forks and cannot be undone by a
dashboard click nobody sees. Disconnecting the project is still the
correct end state and is tracked in #769.

$comment: #1056. This file opens by calling itself the source of truth a human can
read. It accounted for 2 of the 6 rules ruleset 16189198 carries — the
`required_status_checks` rule (the lists above) and the `strict` flag
inside it. The other four gate merges to `main` while emitting no status
context at all, which is why no test could have noticed them missing.
Every entry below is an OBSERVATION, not a declaration: it is not applied
from this file, so on a disagreement the ruleset wins and this section is
the wrong one. Same direction of authority as `strict`, and the same
failure mode — observations go stale silently.
`blocking` means: can this rule alone stop a merge to `main`?
Re-read live with:
gh api repos/bop-clocktower/canary/rulesets/16189198 --jq '.rules'
Last reconciled 2026-09-22. No offline test can discover a rule nobody
wrote down; that line is the step that can.

reason: Blocks deletion of `main` itself. No parameters — the rule is its own
verdict. Blocking because the branch is the thing every other rule in
this ruleset protects; deleting it would take the ruleset with it.
Never exercised in the normal flow, which is precisely why it was
unrecorded: a rule that never fires looks like a rule that is absent.
Blocks force-pushes to `main`, so history cannot be rewritten out
from under a merged commit. Blocking because every status this repo
records — the post-merge detection in `mergePolicy`, the ratchet
baselines, the `External-ID` roadmap links — is keyed to commits that
are assumed to stay put. This is the rule that makes that assumption
true.
Requires a pull request for any change to `main` — including
documentation-only commits — so a direct push is rejected regardless
of actor. Blocking, and the reason `CLAUDE.md` tells every agent to
branch before editing.
The review parameters are the subtle half and are the reason this
rule being unrecorded mattered: a count of 0 read alongside
`require_extra_approval_for_unattributed_changes: true` is not the
whole policy, but on the measured evidence the flag has not bound in
practice. See the `reviews` section below for the effective
requirement and its denominator.
`dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push` and `require_last_push_approval` are
both false, so an approval survives a subsequent push. With `strict`
true, every PR is force-updated against a moving `main`, and each of
those updates is a push — turning either flag on would invalidate
approvals for a reason unrelated to the diff under review.
GitHub's built-in code-quality rule, set to block at `errors`
severity only. Blocking, and it is the one rule in this ruleset that
canary does not produce, configure, or test — it is GitHub's
judgement applied to this repo's diffs, which makes it the rule most
likely to surprise. Recorded here so a merge refused by it has a
written explanation in the repo rather than only on the PR page.
Warnings do not block; only errors do.
Requests an automated review on every non-draft push. NOT blocking:
it produces review comments, not a merge verdict, and
`required_approving_review_count` does not count it. Recorded because
a reviewer seeing an automated review on a PR could reasonably
assume it satisfies something — it does not, and the distinction
between a review that is posted and a review that is required is
exactly the kind of fact this file exists to state.
`review_draft_pull_requests: false` keeps drafts quiet.
The `required` list above IS this rule's context set, and unlike
every other entry in this section the manifest is PRIMARY for it
(ADR 0011) — it is declared here and applied to the ruleset with the
`gh api -X PUT` line in the header. `strict` is recorded and
explained in `mergePolicy` above; it is an observation, not a
declaration, which is how it drifted for three weeks.
`contexts` is a COUNT, not a list, so that the 13 strings live in
exactly one place in this file and cannot disagree with themselves.
The count is 0 and `require_extra_approval_for_unattributed_changes`
is LIVE and TRUE — both verified on the ruleset. What that flag means
is GitHub's definition, not ours: a change is UNATTRIBUTED when its
commit author or committer is not linked to a GitHub account. It is NOT
a synonym for agent- or bot-authored. Commits pushed by the agents that
work in this repo ARE authored by a linked account, so they are
attributed and the flag does not fire on them. An earlier version of
this record asserted the opposite and inferred a policy from it; that
was wrong twice over — wrong definition, and a conclusion nobody had
measured.
MEASURED outcome, with its denominator: of the 25 most recently merged
PRs, 24 merged with ZERO approvals and 1 (#1050) merged with one.
Measured 2026-09-22. `bypass_actors` is empty and
`current_user_can_bypass` is `never`, so those were not admin bypasses —
the rule simply did not demand an approval. Re-measure with:
gh pr list --state merged --limit 25 --json number,reviews --jq '[.[] | {n:.number, approvals: ([.reviews[] | select(.state=="APPROVED")] | length)}]'
So the flag is a LATENT protection that has not bound in practice, not
the everyday requirement. The everyday requirement, on the evidence
above, is 0. Read the two together: `0` is what governs essentially all
traffic here, and the unattributed flag is the floor under the case of
an unlinked-account commit — which the 25-PR window contains no example
of, so its behaviour in this repo is UNMEASURED rather than confirmed.
The `0` is deliberate, not a default (#542 step 4). Single-maintainer
repo: a flat requirement of 1 would mean self-approving every PR, which
trains the reflex the gate exists to prevent. Dropping the unattributed
flag would remove a real protection for the unlinked-commit case, so it
stays. Revisit when a second maintainer joins.
Access posture (#1056) is recorded here rather than in a SECURITY.md
because a reader who finds a review count of 0 needs the collaborator
shape in the same breath, not one file away. Aggregate role counts
only — no account is ever enumerated in this file, and the counts say
nothing about which seats are humans and which are apps. Read live
with:
gh api repos/bop-clocktower/canary/collaborators --jq '[.[].role_name] | group_by(.) | map({role: .[0], count: length})'
Observed 2026-09-22. This is an OBSERVATION; the repo settings win.
